title: Mother of girl killed in Christmas Day fire facing 23 charges
author: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com
content:
Mother of girl killed in Christmas Day fire facing 23 charges

 March 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 1674
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ELKTON — The mother of a 10-year-old girl who was killed in a townhouse fire near Elkton on Christmas morning faces multiple charges — including involuntary manslaughter, child neglect and reckless endangerment — after investigators concluded that hoarding, overloaded electrical outlets and a lack of smoke detectors inside the dwelling were factors in the deadly blaze, according to Cecil County District Court records.For the same alleged reasons, the mother's live-in boyfriend is facing the same 23 criminal charges that have been filed against her, police reported.
Maryland State Police investigators arrested the suspects — Theresa Ann Moats, 40, and Kevin Neal Summerfield, 41, now both of New Castle, Del. — on Friday, March 15, and charged each of them with involuntary manslaughter, neglect of a minor, reckless endangerment and 20 counts of animal cruelty, court records show.
A portion of the charging documents filed against Moats and Summerfield focus on horrid living conditions discovered inside their Willow Drive townhouse where, according to Moats' own admission, as many as 35 pets, mostly dogs and cats, were kept at the same time.
In addition, court records allege that a "vast majority of the floor was covered in caked animal feces" and that the odor of animal urine and feces was pungent throughout the dwelling when Cecil County Department of Animal Services agents responded to that townhouse on Dec. 20 — five days before the fatal fire — after receiving a complaint.
Moats and Summerfield remained in the Cecil County Detention Center on no bond Wednesday night, two days after their bail review hearings, according to court records, which indicate that Cecil County District Court Judge Clara E. Campbell presided over that proceeding. Preliminary hearings for Moats and Summerfield have been set for April 10, court records show.
Moats' daughter — Kyleigh Nicole Treadway — perished in the swift-moving, two-alarm blaze that broke out inside 317 Willow Dr. in the Winding Brook neighborhood, northeast of Elkton, shortly before 7:30 a.m. on Dec. 25, 2023. Kyleigh was trapped inside that burning townhouse after her mother (Moats), her grandmother, her two older brothers and her mother's boyfriend (Summerfield) had escaped.
Court records indicate a woman believed to be Kyleigh's mother approached Capt. William Ryan of Singerly Volunteer Fire Company during the fire and told him that "her baby was right inside the front door."
"Due to the magnitude and intensity of the fire, Ryan and other firefighters were unable to immediately enter the residence to recover the child. When it was safe to enter the residence, Captain Ryan pushed inside the residence and located the deceased child. The child was located near the front door of the residence," according to court records.
An autopsy revealed that Kyleigh's cause of death was listed as smoke inhalation and thermal injuries that included burns covering much of her body, according to police.
Including Kyleigh's five surviving family members, the blaze displaced 17 residents in the three adjacent townhouses damaged by the fire.
POSSIBLE CAUSES
Detectives with the Maryland Office of the State Fire Marshal determined that the blaze that killed Kyleigh started accidentally on the first floor inside an 8'-by-8' room, which was an addition at the rear of the townhouse, and that the cause is either an electric "overload situation based on the multiple operating appliances" or "improperly discarded smoking materials," court records show.
During their investigation, MOSFM investigators discovered multiple electrical power cords connected to one another, which were then all connected to a power strip. The extension cords were wound through the rest of the residence, including around and behind appliances and into the townhouse's backyard.
During her interview with MSP investigators, Moats mentioned the electrical power cords in the backroom where the fire started, police said. Moats said she tried to extinguish the flames after her son woke her up in her second-floor bedroom to alert her about the blaze, police added.
"Theresa observed the 'orange fire' and attempted to put it out using water. Her efforts were in vain. Theresa explained that the backroom was filled with boxes of clothing and miscellaneous items. Among these items was an electrical power cord that was connected to an outside grill. She stated the grill was inoperable. Theresa Moats stated 'this all could have been preventable and that she misses her daughter.' She felt bad and felt it was her fault," according to the charging document.
As for the possibility of improperly discarded smoking materials causing the blaze, investigators noted that they found "several empty Newport cigarette containers and cigarette-style lighters" in that backroom, court records show.
In recorded interviews with MSP investigators, the adults who lived in that Willow Drive townhouse told detectives that smoke detectors had been installed one year before the fire and that they were operational, police said.
However, fire investigators reported that they were unable to locate the remains of any smoke detectors within the townhouse. They further reported that the lack of smoke detectors likely caused a delay in the evacuation of the residence.
In addition, MOSFM detectives reported that they documented "residential hoarding conditions" inside the Willow Court townhouse during their investigation. Specifically, the detectives cited an "overabundance of combustibles and clothing" in the living room, in the dining/kitchen area and in the rear backroom where the fire started, noting that they removed large trash bags of clothing from there and that a connecting storage closet also was filled with combustibles, court records show.
Court records further state that the poor conditions of the home, the amount of 'hoarding', as well as the widespread animal waste and overabundance of trash and other combustibles — combined with the lack of smoke detection — likely delayed and hampered the home's evacuation.
ANIMAL SERVICES INVESTIGATION
Charging documents indicate that two Cecil County Department of Animal Services officers went to 317 Willow Dr. on Dec. 20 — five days before the fatal fire there — and impounded 18 animals — 14 dogs and four cats — that showed signs of neglect and abuse, after receiving a call regarding "multiple canines of various ages located within the residence," court records show.
The officers heard "excessive barking" when they knocked on the door, which continued when Summerfield let them inside the dwelling, police said. Once inside, police added, the officers "detected the smell of animal urine and feces."
Court records allege that the officers observed eight pit bull mixed puppies of "average health and slightly underweight" crated without food and water. Officers also saw eight adult canines of mixed breeds and several cats of various ages inside the townhouse, court records show.
The officers further reported that a vast majority of the floor was covered in caked animal waste. Officers informed Moats and Summerfield that their animals could not remain in such conditions, resulting in several animals being surrendered to the officers. Officers reported that the surrendered puppies immediately ran to empty water bowls and attempted to drink after they were uncrated.
"When the officers arrived at the animal shelter, two emaciated puppies were found to be very dehydrated and needed subcutaneous fluids. All puppies ate and drank ravenously. Two crates of puppies each drank an entire bucket of water," according to the charging documents.
During interviews with police, Summerfield, Moats and Moats' mother admitted that not all of the pets had been vaccinated; that the dogs urinated and defecated inside the townhouse "all the time;" and that the cats would "urinate and defecate everywhere and it would get on Kyleigh's clothes," court records show. Summerfield acknowledged to investigators that the "pet situation" was "ridiculous" and excessive, police reported.
After they impounded the 18 animals from that Willow Drive townhouse, the Animal Services officers "planned to make a report to Child Protective Services, as the children in the home were subjected to poor living conditions," according to the charging documents.
SIGNS AT SCHOOL
On Jan. 11, some 17 days after the fatal fire, an MSP investigator and a Cecil County Department of Social Services supervisor went to Cecil Manor Elementary School in Elk Mills, where Kyleigh had been a fourth-grade student, and interviewed her teachers, guidance and school nurse — all of whom cited signs of possible child neglect, court records show.
According to the charging document, school officials were concerned over Kyleigh's hygiene, reporting that her hair and clothes would often emanate smells of animal waste. School officials also noted that other students in her class would avoid Kyleigh due to the smell of her clothes.
The school nurse routinely washed Kyleigh's clothes and washed and brushed the girl's hair on multiple occasions because it was "matted, itchy and foul-smelling," police said. Staff members replaced Kyleigh's backpack twice because cats at her residence urinated and vomited on top of her previous backpacks, police added.
"Kyleigh's hygiene issues were described as 'terrible' and they needed to be addressed 3-4 times per day. Kyleigh stated to teachers that she had a 'ton' of pets and that she loved them," court records allege.
Court records allege that school staff attempted to contact Moats by email and by phone, but there was "absolutely no involvement to address concern brought forth by the school," including the concerns that Kyleigh was "disoriented during school and not mentally present," that she never completed homework assignments, and that she was academically performing at a level several years behind her peers.
School staff members alleged that Moats "showed a lack of care for Kyleigh," according to the charging documents, which also indicate that "daily communication logs were sent home and they were never signed or acknowledged by Kyleigh's guardians."
School officials told investigators that referrals were made to the Department of Social Services after Kyleigh moved with her family from Delaware and started attending Cecil Manor Elementary School and that the school provided a "vast amount of support to Kyleigh and her family."
In one section of the charging documents, it reads, "Prior to Christmas 2023, the school counselor visited Kyleigh's residence to drop off food and presents. The occupants (guardians) were unable to open the front door fully. Without stepping inside the residence, the school counselor could smell animal urine and feces emanating from the inside. Animal feces were observed on the floor of the residence when the door was ajar."

 Being a good Catholic does not mean turning one's head to crime committed by priests or anyone else.My six siblings and I were fortunate to attend Catholic School. As adult professionals, we credit the nuns with our integrity.
All the nuns at our school were strong women. They were tough Germans who fled Germany as Adolf Hitler came to power. I stayed in touch with many of the nuns over the years.
Due to their background, they insisted that we look out for one another, for protecting each other, and correcting any aspect of life that would place one in a harmful situation. Sitting down when seeing evil was not an option for them.
It is that teaching that brought me to reporting a priest in our Maryland parish for inappropriate contact with small boys in 1987. Seeing things with my own eyes, I reached out to one of the nuns that I trusted. The parish settled the cases, and the priest was defrocked.
Defrocked. Removed for good. He would have no more Catholic school playgrounds to select his next victim nor another innocent parent to convince that his or her child spend the night with him in the rectory.
Last year at Eastertime, the Maryland Attorney General released a report on the sexual abuse of children within the Baltimore Archdiocese. Due to the stigma of sexual assaults especially for boys, it is impossible to calibrate the exact number of victims.
That report sat poorly with one of the local devout Catholics. She seemed to not understand why the state of Maryland would increase the statute of limitations for child victims. She condemned the amount of money available to the victims and categorically and alarmingly published, while defending the church, false statements: "No new cases have been brought up for over 25 years and most of the clergy who were involved are not even alive today."
That is like stating a crime like drunk driving has been extinguished throughout the country in the last 25 years.
The upset parishioner is considered one of the pillars of the church. Thus, she has a good vantage point to observe. With that comes duty. And one of the duties is to take the blinders off, get educated on child victims and report any inappropriate conduct upon a child. That makes us good Catholics because praying alone does not extinguish pedophilia.
CATHY LINDBERG JAROSZ
Easton

title: Eclipse 2024: Extra police, even National Guard troops being deployed amid alerts, government warnings
author: Mike Sunnucks APG National Enterprise Editor
content:
Eclipse 2024: Extra police, even National Guard troops being deployed amid alerts, government warnings

 March 25, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Mike Sunnucks APG National Enterprise Editor | Section: Eclipse 
 
 1068
 Words 

 Read News Document

 More police will be deployed, some National Guard troops are being activated and put at the ready and emergency orders along with aviation alerts have been issued for the total solar eclipse set to sweep across the U.S. on Monday, April 8.The eclipse will be visible across the continental U.S. with a swath of the country — from Texas to New England — experiencing as much as four minutes of daytime darkness with the moon blocking the sun.
Eclipse day and the weekend leading up to are expected to be one of the busiest travel periods in U.S. history.
That is prompting concerns about traffic congestion and how the events and expected high usage rates will impact internet and other communications connections including electronic transactions and payment systems.
Gasoline supplies could be impacted in prime viewing regions.
TROOPS ACTIVATED
The Oklahoma National Guard is activating troops from a civil support unit to assist local government agencies during the eclipse. That includes members of a hazardous materials team.
The Oklahoma guard said March 18 it received a request for resources from the McCurtain County Emergency Management agency.
The state is in the path of totality where the moon will completely shield the sun on April 8.
Oklahoma officials expect as many 100,000 visitors to McCurtain County in the southeastern part of the state. The county, which has a population of approximately 31,000 people, is part of the sprawling Choctaw Nation Indian territory. The tribe is hosting a number of eclipse events.
"McCurtain County Emergency Management requested our support because they expect up to 100,000 additional people visiting their communities to watch the eclipse," said Lt. Col. Jabonn Flurry, an Oklahoma National Guard commander. "This influx of visitors has the potential to overtax local resources and thanks to the training and experience our Guardsmen have working alongside local agencies all across Oklahoma, the (Civil Support Team) is uniquely qualified to support our fellow Oklahomans."
Other states are deploying more state police and have National Guard troops and resources at the ready for the eclipse.
"The New York National Guard is prepared to provide troops and two of our Naval Militia patrol boats if required," said Eric Durr, public affairs director of the New York State Division of Military and Naval Affairs.
Durr said the Empire State's homeland security agency has not yet tasked the Guard with any eclipse-related deployments.
The eclipse's totality path will go through upstate New York including Rochester, Buffalo and Niagara Falls.
The New York State Police is implementing emergency plans and will deploy more troopers statewide for the eclipse, the agency announced Monday, March 25.
In Arkansas, the state's National Guard was part of pre-eclipse training exercises March 13 with state emergency managers and police. Arkansas' emergency control center will be activated April 6 through April 10.
The state expects as many as 1.5 million visitors for the eclipse and another 500,000 Arkansans traveling to areas of totality.
POLICE PRESENCE
Local police, state highway patrols and other law enforcement and emergency agencies across the country are planning for increased patrols, staffing and deployments for the celestial event.
"We will have additional staffing working the day of the eclipse in order to have more resources available since there will be additional people in the city," said Stan Reno, chief of police in Carbondale, Illinois, in the southern part of the state.
Reno does not expect additional state resources.
In Texas, which is viewed as a prime eclipse viewing spot in the U.S. because of its comparatively clearer skies than other totality locations, police, emergency and transportation managers are preparing for a deluge of visitors and in-state travelers to view the events.
More than 1 million people could visit the state, according to the Texas Department of Transportation.
"The public should expect a police presence on our roadways and across the city, the day of the event," said Jennifer Pryor, a public information officer with the Dallas Police Department.
"While the department is working to keep our roadways and streets safe during the eclipse, the public should be prepared for increased traffic and delays. Traffic may impact all areas of DFW (Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport), not just the city of Dallas. Plan extra time for your travels," she said.
Sgt. Tyler Ross, a spokesperson for the Ohio Highway Patrol, said there will be more police out for the eclipse and like other police warns motorists not to stop on the side of highways to view the astronomical event.
"Leading up to, during and after the eclipse, our troopers will be highly visible, enforcing all traffic laws and ready to assist, ensuring traffic flows smoothly and everyone enjoys this rare event safely," Ross said. "Remember, stopping on the side of roads or exit ramps for viewing is prohibited and unsafe."
The eclipse will be the largest such event in the U.S. since 1806. There will not be another total solar eclipse in the U.S. until 2044.
Social media buzz about the eclipse is on the rise including its technological, public safety, natural, spiritual and metaphysical impacts.
EMERGENCY ALERTS
A number of governments in Texas, Ohio and other states in the totality path have issued special and emergency orders related to the eclipse.
A special eclipse order issued by March 13 Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine's order instructs state agencies, including police, to prepare for the event and for those traveling for it to make sure to carry cash, cell phone chargers, blankets and other items.
Bell County, Texas, which expects 400,000 visitors for the eclipse (doubling its population) has declared a state of emergency for the event, urging residents to stock up on fuel, drug prescriptions and groceries before the influx of tourists and potential impacts.
Other emergency and tourism agencies are recommending having cash on hand, fueling up on gas and stocking up on food and other staples before the April event in case of disruptions. Protective eyewear is also required to view the eclipse.
The Federal Aviation Administration has issued a special alert for airlines and general aviation pilots for the April 8 eclipse.
That includes warnings of increased aviation traffic — especially in the prime path — and that there could be flight restrictions or changes ordered by the U.S. military or security agencies.
That could especially impact air travel and airports in areas such as Dallas, Houston, Little Rock, Arkansas; Indianapolis, Cleveland, Buffalo and Burlington, Vermont, according to the FAA.
"There may be a higher traffic volume than normal anticipated at airports along the path of the eclipse. Traffic should anticipate delays during peak traffic periods," the FAA said in its alert.

title: Dundalk residents view crumpled bridge with shock, dismay
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Dundalk residents view crumpled bridge with shock, dismay

 March 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: State News 
 
 667
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DUNDALK — A few hours after Teresita Santana and her family drove across the Francis Scott Key Bridge, they felt their house shake."As if something had exploded," Santana said.
Santana and her family, including her children and mother, got back to their home in Dundalk late Monday night after a trip to Washington, D.C., to get their passports and see the cherry blossoms. It was only a few hours after they crossed the Key Bridge on their way home that the bridge collapsed.
A container ship slammed into the iconic bridge just before 1:30 a.m. Tuesday. Within seconds, the bridge crumpled into the chilly waters of the Patapsco River at the entrance to the Baltimore Harbor.
In the hours that followed, authorities began search and rescue efforts for survivors of the collapse. Radar indicated that vehicles had been discovered at the bottom of the river, which is about 50 feet deep.
By Tuesday evening, officials said that six construction workers who had been repairing potholes on the bridge at the time of the collapse had been presumed dead. Two construction workers were rescued in the efforts.
Tuesday morning, Santana looked out on the now collapsed bridge from a hill on Dundalk Avenue, across the street from the Logan Village Shopping Center.
"It was scary because it could have been us," Santana said.
Santana wasn't the only one looking at what's left of the I-695 bridge. People filtered in and out Tuesday morning to see it for themselves. "Shock" was a word repeated often.
"Shock and dismay," were the words Judy Corkhum used to describe the emotions of residents she had talked to.
"Nobody in a million years thought we would wake up this morning to something like that," said Corkhum, who also viewed the collapsed bridge from off Dundalk Avenue. "It brings back emotions from 9/11. ... You saw that and the first thing you think is, 'Oh my god. The people. The workers.'"
Corkhum, who recently moved to Baltimore from Dundalk, said she heard about the bridge collapse via a text from a neighbor at 4 a.m. Tuesday. She said her friend's son, a truck driver, "literally just got over the bridge before it happened."
"She said, 'I was having a heart attack this morning thinking he was out on the road last night,'" Corkhum said.
Corkhum said her friend went into surgery this morning, so she was happy to know her son was OK.
Anthony Meeks, a Dundalk native, said he heard about the collapse as soon as he woke up.
"The Key Bridge is a very iconic piece of Dundalk," he said. "It's something that everybody who's from Dundalk or this city even has at one point in their life crossed."
Meeks remembers being scared to cross the bridge when he was younger. These days, he crosses it every two weeks.
"It (will) make me go out of my way to find a different path to get to where I need to go," he said about the collapse. "It could make my trips be a lot longer."
Meeks called the incident an eye opener.
"Because it's like you don't really expect these kinds of tragedies and stuff to happen and occur in your neighborhood," he said.
Dundalk-Patapsco Neck Historical Society President Jean Walker said this is the first time Dundalk has experienced a large disaster like this.
Historical Society Vice President Joe Stadler called the event "unbelievable."
"It takes a while to fathom it," he said.
For both Walker and Stadler, the bridge has been a big part of Dundalk. They said the founder of the Historical Society, Ben Womer, was "instrumental" in getting the bridge named after Francis Scott Key, the author of the national anthem.
"It's the backdrop for everything around here," Stadler said about the bridge.
Standing on the hill, looking at the wreckage of the bridge, Corkhum said she had to make the trip from her new home in Baltimore to see what had happened with her own eyes.
"I'm so used to seeing that pretty view out there every day," she said. "It's going to be horrible seeing that (there's) no view anymore."

title: A massive disaster stuns Dundalk residents
author: JIM JOHNSON
content:
A massive disaster stuns Dundalk residents

 March 31, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: JIM JOHNSON | Section: Columns 
 
 648
 Words 

 Read News Document

 I was in Dundalk the morning the Francis Scott Key Bridge collapsed. APG Chesapeake owns the newspaper in Dundalk on the east side of the bridge. Star Democrat reporter Maggie Trovato and I traveled to help the newspaper with its coverage of the disaster.Two observations.
First, people in Dundalk had stunned looks on their faces that day. The bridge was iconic, a fixture on the city skyline. In an instant, it was gone. The shock was palpable, easily seen in the vacant stares of people who realized their lives would change but without yet fully understanding how.
Second, the scale of the disaster was massive. Photos cannot capture the size of the bridge structure nor the size of the ship that brought the bridge down. Seeing it from Dundalk, you begin to comprehend the challenging job ahead to simply clear the debris and reopen Baltimore Harbor.
Kudos to the Commissioners of St. Michaels for apologizing after approving a permit for a Makers Market to host a vendor event at Muskrat Park. City code prohibits the use of the park for for-profit ventures. Another code prohibits the use of tents on the park's lawns.
"We apologize that it was an oversight previously," Commission President David Breimhurst said. "And I can tell you that the staff is well aware of what the issue was. These permits will be thoroughly vetted in the future before they come to us."
Yes, someone should have known about the ordinances that limit the use of the park. Yet the commission should be applauded for trying to find a solution to help artists and crafters to move to a more desirable location, an event that brings hundreds of visitors to St. Michaels each year.
At the commission's March 13 meeting, Trish Payne and Mark Montoya, members of Talbot County's local art community, requested the use of the park every other Saturday or every second Sunday starting in April for a local art vendors event.
There was vocal opposition by members of the St. Michaels Business Association, who said that the vendor event could harm to local businesses.
After a heated discussion by members of the public, the commissioners approved the event on a trial run to begin in April to assess impacts to the local community.
That decision had to be reversed after the discovery of the city codes sections prohibiting the type of event Makers Market wishes to hold.
Too frequently these days government agencies dig their heels into the sand and refuse to budge, even when they are in the wrong. The apology from the commissioners was refreshing.
* * * * *
A sad anniversary passed on Friday. It's been one year since Russian authorities arrested Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich, falsely accusing him of being a spy. Much of the time he has been held in a tiny cell, awaiting a trial that has not yet been set.
Gershkovich was doing his job, reporting on news, helping readers understand what is happening in the authoritarian-run Russia. His arrest and detention shows the importance of freedom of the press and the dangers that authoritarian governments bring to people's freedoms. Those freedoms are in jeopardy all over the world as authoritarian regimes rise.
It is important to remember the role that reporters perform in a free society. Journalism is not a crime.
* * * * *

title: Effects from New Jersey earthquake felt across Mid-Shore
author: Staff Writer

Effects from New Jersey earthquake felt across Mid-Shore

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: News

 EASTON — From Glen Burnie to Chestertown, trembles were felt from this morning's 4.7 magnitude earthquake. Officials from the U.S. Geological Survey said residents across the Northeast reported rumbling in a region where people are unaccustomed to feeling the ground move.The agency reported a quake at 10:23 a.m. with a preliminary magnitude of 4.8, centered near Lebanon, New Jersey, or about 45 miles west of New York City and 50 miles north of Philadelphia. USGS figures indicated that the quake might have been felt by more than 42 million people.
Across social media, users from Crumpton, Centreville, Worton, Ridgely, Wye Mills and Easton felt the quake. In Chester, one woman reported small vibration, less than 10 seconds. Melonie Mattison of Kent Island said she was sitting at here dining table when the chair wobbled.
For most though, unless they were sitting still it was an easy to miss experience here on the Shore. As Justin Davis quipped, "I felt more trembles when a tractor trailer passes by."
The shaking stirred memories of the Aug. 23, 2011, earthquake that jolted tens of millions of people from Georgia to Canada. Registering magnitude 5.8, it was the strongest quake to hit the East Coast since World War II. The epicenter was in Virginia.
That earthquake left cracks in the Washington Monument, spurred the evacuation of the White House and Capitol and rattled New Yorkers three weeks before the 10th anniversary of the Sept. 11 terror attacks.
Earthquakes are less common on this side of the U.S. because the East Coast does not lie on a boundary of tectonic plates. But East Coast quakes can still pack a punch — its rocks are better at spreading earthquake energy across far distances.
"If we had the same magnitude quake in California, it probably wouldn't be felt nearly as far away," said U.S.G.S. geophysicist Paul Caruso.
The White House said in a statement that President Joe Biden had been briefed on the earthquake and was "in touch with federal, state, and local officials as we learn more."
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

 An earthquake shook Maryland Friday morning, with residents across the region reporting rumbling in an area where people are unaccustomed to feeling the ground move.The U.S. Geological Survey reported a quake at 10:23 a.m. with a preliminary magnitude of 4.8, centered near Lebanon, N.J., or about 45 miles west of New York City and 50 miles north of Philadelphia. USGS figures indicated that the quake might have been felt by more than 42 million people.
Across social media, users from Crumpton, Centreville, Worton, Ridgely, Wye Mills and Easton felt the quake. In Chester, one woman reported small vibration, less than 10 seconds. Melonie Mattison of Kent Island said she was sitting at here dining table when the chair wobbled.
For most though, unless they were sitting still, it was an easy to miss experience here on the Shore. As Justin Davis quipped, "I felt more trembles when a tractor trailer passes by."
The shaking stirred memories of the Aug. 23, 2011, earthquake that jolted tens of millions of people from Georgia to Canada. Registering magnitude 5.8, it was the strongest quake to hit the East Coast since World War II. The epicenter was in Virginia.
In Newark, Delaware, Friday morning, dozens of readers told the Newark Post they felt the shaking.
"My house shook," one person said. Another reported "a rumble and a strange noise." On Old Paper Mill Road, a resident said her walls and floors were shaking.
Ann Marie Drozdick was in her apartment at Regency Square Apartments near Fairfield when the earthquake struck.
"The whole place was shaking," Drozdick said. "It was shaking and shivering. The dishes and everything were shaking."
At first she wasn't sure what was happening.
"It didn't last too long, 30 seconds, and then it stopped," she said. "I went out in the hallway and the neighbor said it's an earthquake."
Amtrak said it was inspecting its tracks Friday and had speed restrictions in place throughout the busy Northeast Corridor. New Jersey Transit posted on X that its train system was subject to delays caused by bridge inspections. The Philadelphia area's PATCO rail line suspended service out of what it said was "an abundance of caution."
Earthquakes are less common on this side of the U.S. because the East Coast does not lie on a boundary of tectonic plates. But East Coast quakes can still pack a punch — its rocks are better at spreading earthquake energy across far distances.
"If we had the same magnitude quake in California, it probably wouldn't be felt nearly as far away," said U.S.G.S. geophysicist Paul Caruso.
Hannah Combs from the Bay Times and Record Observer, Josh Shannon from the Newark Post and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Kent Island Giving Circle presents funding for vets
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Kent Island Giving Circle presents funding for vets

 April 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 909
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTER — It's always the season of giving for the Kent Island Giving Circle, which met to hear presentations from organizations seeking funding April 1 at the Four Seasons Club House at Kent Island.More than just donating money, the mission of the Giving Circle is "to educate ourselves to the local needs of the community and leverage our collective resources to support those needs," organizer Rona Sue Warner said.
"It's about education as much as giving," she said.
Every October and April, three local organizations present to the group, introduce who they are, and demonstrate how their needs support the community.
The 30 members of the Giving Circle collectively donate $100 each, twice a year to a Queen Anne's County charity and following presentations, votes are cast for which organization to present the collected money to.
This session's $3,000 funding was awarded to the Veteran and Military Support Alliance (VAMSA) for their work supporting local veterans and their loved ones and addressing PTSD.
VAMSA Executive Director Eric Johnson presented information on the work of the local open resource center for vets, families and their caregivers.
Johnson was driven by his own experiences as a United States Air Force veteran returning home from active service and noted the importance of streamlining finding help for himself and others.
"I have lived a life of service," he said.
The mission of VAMSA is to "operationalize thank you for your service" and provide a way to meet needs as they are presented, according to Johnson.
Picking up where the Veterans Affairs can't, VAMSA provides local resources to veterans, families and caregivers, including claims support, wellness programs, housing and education assistance and like minded support groups.
Identifying how service related conditions and disabilities develop further down the line, VAMSA is also looking out for the next generation of veterans by teaching at college ROTC classes.
In 2023 VAMSA's Suicide Saves prevention program saved recorded several lives saved with its suicide prevention program, according to Johnson.
With the Giving Circle's funding, VAMSA will seek additional training for its volunteers, the majority who are veterans themselves, "who bring a wealth of experiences," he said.
Eventually VAMSA would like to build a nationally recognized organization, Johnson said, but for now they are proud to continually help one local veteran at a time.
More information about VAMSA, including a complete list of services, can be found at qacveteransupport.org.
Also presenting their mission to the Giving Circle was Scott Lockerman and his Belgian Malinois Khari of the Maryland Police K9 Foundation. This organization seeks to equip K9 units in underfunded police departments and keep them outfitted, equipped and trained, Lockerman said.
Police K9s are an investment and a benefit to communities as a preventative measure to help deter crime and scoop out drugs, he said.
"We are committed to providing for the needs of active duty K9s as well as the needs of those K9s that have retired," Lockerman said.
Fully trained police canines can cost between $16,000 and $20,000 that not all police departments can afford, not to mention additional safety costs of ballistic vests, heat alarms for patrol vehicles and other preventatives to keep dogs safe, he said.
Queen Anne's County does not currently have a canine unit and the Maryland Police K9 Foundation is steadily looking to change that, he said.
The K9 Foundation aims to eventually have a brick and mortar building available for training, he said.
More information about the Maryland K9 Foundation can be found at mdpk9f.org.
The other presentation to the Giving Circle was Project Linus, committed to embracing the art of sewing and the act of service, this is an organization dedicated to providing handmade "blanket hugs" to children.
Project Linus is a national organization, but each chapter is responsible for the distribution of its own local blankets and the Maryland Mid Shore Chapter has supplied over 4,200 blankets to Queen Anne's, Kent, Talbot and Caroline counties since its inception in 2016, according to Maryland Mid Shore Chapter Coordinator Kim Couch.
Project Linus partners with numerous children programs including local hospitals and foster care agencies to supply handcrafted blankets and "give them something that's theirs they can carry with."
"Even hospitals that don't have a pediatric unit, kids come into the ER all the time," she said.
The group is entirely self-funded and is always collecting materials of yarn, thread, scissors and more, as well as monetary donations.
"Basically anything you can think of to make a blanket," she said.
"Blanketeers" from all over the region meet monthly for Make a Blanket Day and all ages are welcome to gather, hone their quilting craft and inspire future generations of knitting enthusiasts.
"Passing along that knowledge and helping children is very important to us," Couch said.
More information about Project Linus can be found at www.projectlinus.org.
Members note it is never an easy decision to vote for compelling worthwhile organizations presenting to the Giving Circle time after time.
"The power of group giving is that it opens the possibilities," member Kathy Sells, of Kent Island said.
"It's always hard to make a final decision," she said.
Even for organizations not chosen for funding, the Giving Circle gives members the opportunity to learn about local worthwhile organizations they might not have known about right in their backyard and to pass along that knowledge to others.
"All the groups were wonderful. We're all so impressed," Warner said.
The Kent Island Giving Circle meets every October and April to consider organizations for donations.
The Giving Circle is currently in the process of developing a website and more information about how to get involved can be found by contacting Warner at warneronthebay@atlanticbb.net.

title: No vote on bill
author: Staff Writer
content:
No vote on bill

 April 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 379
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Did you know that in the state of Maryland, you can cause a motor vehicle collision due to reckless or negligent driving that results in the death of another person, and never have to go to court? You can simply prepay a traffic ticket.Again in 2024, a change was proposed with a bill that was cross-filed in both the Senate and House. (SB68/HR1335) Reckless and Negligent Driving — Death of Another — Must Appear Violation (Sherry's and Christian's Law).
"Providing that a person charged with reckless or negligent driving must appear in court and may not prepay the fine if the reckless or negligent driving contributed to an accident that resulted in the death of another person, unless a court for good cause shown waives the requirement to appear."
Sounds like a no-brainer, right?
If you take a life, you must appear in court. For the past two years, a version of this same bill has passed unanimously through the Senate, both in committee and on the Senate floor. But it never made it through the House Judiciary Committee.
This year, the bill was cross-filed and given a hearing in both the Senate Judicial Proceedings Committee and the House Judiciary Committee where it again saw no opposition. But don't assume that it will become law. After countless hours of writing, reading, discussing, and holding hearings in both houses, a bill that is so straightforward it had no opposition, never got a vote on either side this year. To be clear, it wasn't that it didn't pass, it just was never voted on.
In a state with a 90-day legislative session, time is precious. Not only is it a shame that this bill didn't get passed but think of all the wasted time. How many other important bills were never even heard this year while countless hours were spent on bills that never got voted on? To say that this is frustrating is certainly an understatement. To all those that traveled to Annapolis every Monday night to rally support, attended committee hearings, wrote letters and made telephone calls; your dedication and hard work are appreciated.
Del. Luke Clippinger, chair, House Judiciary Committee (Baltimore City) and Sen. William C. Smith Jr., chair, Senate Judicial Proceedings Committee (Montgomery County), you can and must do better.
MARIANNE JACKSON
Queen Anne

title: Bill seeks to provide online protection for children
author: Matt Wynn mwynn@somdnews.com
content:
Bill seeks to provide online protection for children

 April 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Matt Wynn mwynn@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 367
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Maryland legislators are heading a nation-leading effort to protect children and their data online.The Maryland Kids Code — a bill sent to the governor's desk after unanimous votes from the House and Senate on its third reading — seeks to afford protections to children from all online products they are likely to access.
The bill states that entities that develop and provide online services and products that children are reasonably likely to access shall ensure the best interests of children when designing, developing and providing those products.
Currently, 75% of the top social media platforms use AI to recommend children's profiles to strangers, according to the Maryland Kids Code Coalition's website. One in three of the top 100 free apps on the Google Play store have banner ads, including ads for adult content, the website says.
According to the Pew Research Center, in 2022, 97% of American teenagers aged 13–17 used the internet every day, with 46% responding they used the internet almost constantly.
Del. C. T. Wilson (D-Charles) was one of the sponsors of the bill.
"Tonight's vote is a landmark moment for Maryland kids and families working toward a better, safer online world," said Todd Minor Sr. and Mia Minor, parent advocates from Accokeek who founded the Matthew E. Minor Awareness Foundation. "We've worked hard for this moment, and we're super proud our legislators had the courage and determination to stand up to the Big Tech lobbyists in the hope that other families will never have to suffer pain like ours has endured."
The Matthew E. Minor Awareness Foundation was created after Matthew Minor died at 12 years old as a result of the "choking/black-out" challenge that had been circulating on social media and other internet platforms.
"Today's vote shows support for the Kids Code model's safety-by-design and privacy-by-default principles that transcends political divides, reflecting growing public recognition of the urgent need for smart, effective policy solutions to protect kids online," Maryland Kids Code Coalition spokeswoman Marisa Shea of St. Mary's County said.
The bill has wide-reaching support, with organizations like the Digital Harbor Foundation, the Free State PTA, the Maryland Association of School Health Nurses, the Maryland Coalition of Families and the Maryland State Education Association testifying in favor of it.

 Five out-of-state individuals — four men and a woman — have been charged with felony theft following an alleged theft of nearly $8,000 worth of merchandise from Ulta Beauty in Prince Frederick.The incident occurred on April 4 at approximately 4:37 p.m., according to the Calvert County Sheriff's Office. Deputies responded to the store when a call went out that a theft had occurred.
According to a sheriff's office report, "Two males and one female entered the store and placed numerous colognes and perfumes into bags and fled the store. After fleeing the store, witnesses observed all three suspects enter a gray Mercury Montego that fled northbound on Route 4."
According to court documents filed by Deputy Antonio Tavares, Deputy Justin MacWilliams located the Mercury traveling northbound on Route 4, which then turned onto Route 2.
MacWilliams "initiated a traffic stop in the area of Pushaw Station Road in Sunderland. During the traffic stop, five occupants were located in the suspect vehicle along with numerous bags of perfumes and colognes in plain view. The total value of the stolen items was approximately $7,694 dollars."
In addition to the merchandise that was allegedly stolen from the Prince Frederick store, Tavares reported in charging papers that several cellphones were also confiscated.
The five arrested are identified as Yeiner Jose Rodriguez Barcelo, 27, of Bronx, N.Y., Yoncar Alberto Rainoso, 21, of Manhattan, N.Y., Estefani Andrea Urbano-Zapata, 21, of Cape Girardea, Mo., Raimil Marquez Jimenez, 25, of Washington, D.C., and Adony Josue Carana, 27, of Manhattan N.Y.
A sheriff's office press release stated that further investigation revealed Rodriguez-Barcelo was wanted on an open warrant from Pennsylvania for felony retail theft related to thefts at Ulta stores in Pennsylvania.
Court records show Carana, who was also listed with the alias Carrano, has been released after posting $10,000 bond. As of Monday, the other four remained at the Calvert detention center on a no-bond status.
A district court hearing on the charges the five are facing is scheduled for June 3. Language interpreters have been requested for four of the five defendants, court records show.
The Prince Frederick Ulta has been the scene of similar thefts over the last three years. Other Ulta stores regionally and nationally have been targets of alleged thieves. Several national news outlets have reported allegations of a possible retail theft ring in the state of California. The alleged perpetrators there stole $8 million in cosmetics from several chains, including Ulta, and then sold the products on Amazon.
It is not known at this time if the five arrested in Calvert last week are part of a larger theft ring.
Calvert County Sheriff Ricky Cox (R) issued a note of thanks in an agency press release to "the witnesses on scene that went above and beyond to promptly call 911 and provide details of the suspects and suspects' vehicle. Your efforts are greatly appreciated."

title: Workshop encourages becoming an informed weather spotter
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Workshop encourages becoming an informed weather spotter

 April 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 696
 Words 

 Read News Document

 For Warning Coordinator Meteorologist for the National Weather Service, Sarah Johnson, discussing weather's not just typical small talk.She deals in tornados, hail, high winds and severe storms all the time. As Marylanders escape winter weather, hopefully, there's a pause in the storm seasons.
June is considered the beginning of hurricane season and Johnson mentioned some things to stay alert to on the Eastern Shore.
At the Kent County Public Library on March 21, she introduced her audience to their program: SKYWARN.
She's looking for more and more people to become a spotter, who look out for the basics of thunderstorm development, storm structure and severe weather features, then report the information accurately.
"The main mission of the spotter is to be aware of the rapidly changing conditions of the weather," Johnson replied.
And it's sorely needed too.
Johnson said last year they reported the second most severe thunderstorms.
The third most for tornado warnings.
And the fourth most in flash flood warnings.
Unperturbed by the smaller audience in attendance, she was concise and enthusiastic while walking through the process of what to look out for.
For instance, people tend to be on high alert when they get something on their phone saying "tornado warning." Not so much when they get a "severe thunderstorm warning."
"That's a mistake to think one's worse than the other," Johnson commented.
Especially when water can be more harmful than wind in most cases, she said.
"When we look at the fatalities, 75% in the United States are due to water in some way; 50% of those are those are due to storm surge; 25% freshwater heavy rain flooding. Keep that in mind. Don't think, 'Oh, it's just a tropical storm.' No, you still need to pay attention and see what the hazards are."
Severe storms should not be treated much differently than a tornado.
She then pointed out the difference between a storm watch and a storm warning. A watch means to keep an eye on the weather pattern.
A warning means, don't just watch — get prepared.
A severe storm warning means, gather up some candles for light, or buy extra gas for the back-up generator and do things that will prepare your family and yourself for a potential hazard.
As hurricanes emerge from the North Atlantic ocean and the Gulf of Mexico, Johnson reminded her audience how to categorize them and what that exactly means.
Hurricanes, big or small, she indicated, can create problems, such as tornados.
The uninformed, she added, might hear about a category 1 hurricane and think it's not much of a problem. They'll see it as a little rain and wind. Very minimal damage.
The savvy spotter though, will see that even a category 1 hurricane can create big problems, such as a tornado. The spotter will know category 1, simply describes the wind of the hurricane. Nothing else. It does not highlight the possibility of it creating tornados or other adverse weather conditions.
And those who think tornados are only a threat in Kansas are in for a rude awakening.
Tornados hit everywhere, Johnson pointed out. Even in our backyard.
She said Hurricane Ida was a remnant tropical system that produced a lot of tornados in 2020.
Hurricane Isaias was a destructive Category 1 hurricane, producing the longest tracked tornado in Delaware history.
Tornados in Cecil County and Southern Delaware — resulted in fatalities last year.
"That's why we need you all," she said, encouraging her audience to report their observations to their nearest national weather station.
To become a spotter, adults are invited to complete the SKYWARN training.
Those who finish the course join a volunteer program with between 350,000 and 400,000 trained severe weather spotters.
Individuals affiliated with hospitals, schools, churches and nursing homes or who have a responsibility for protecting others are encouraged to become a spotter.
"There can be no finer reward than to know that your efforts have given your family and neighbors the precious gift of time—minutes that can help save lives," as stated by the NWS.
And as the movie "Twisters," the sequel to the original from 1996, comes out in theaters shortly, Johnson jokes that she's preparing to field a lot more questions about tornados.
She discouraged the crowd on becoming storm chasers like sensationalist Hollywood actors and actresses, but rather to become informed citizens who save lives.

title: Caroline County residents show support for child abuse prevention with pinwheels
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Caroline County residents show support for child abuse prevention with pinwheels

 April 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 606
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Four years since the first Pinwheels for Prevention planting ceremony in Caroline County, the number of shiny blue and silver pinwheels twirling in the breeze has grown.For the event, hosted by CASA of Caroline every year, the pinwheels are placed on lawns and in gardens throughout the county to spread awareness of child abuse and promote its prevention. CASA of Caroline Executive Director Amy Horne said the blue in the pinwheels represents the color of bruises, and the pinwheels themselves "represent the whimsical, carefree childhood that all kids deserve."
At the annual planting ceremony on Fourth Street in Denton on April 10, Horne said participation has grown throughout the county in the past four years.
"My gosh, go up to the Town of Ridgely," she said in an interview. "They have an amazing display."
CASA of Caroline is a nonprofit organization that advocates for and helps find homes for abused and neglected children.
On the nonprofit's website, there is a virtual garden that shows where many of the pinwheels have been planted this year. Horn said hundreds of pinwheels have been planted.
In the 20 years the organization has been around, it has advocated for more than 100 children in the county, Horne said.
"People may think (that because) we're a close-knit county, that it doesn't happen here, but it does," she said about child abuse. "With the tremendous outpouring of support — as you can see here, and that we receive all over the county — it's obvious that Caroline County is really committed to being a safe place for children and families."
CASA of Caroline Board President Keith Johnson talked about the different agencies and organizations that are involved when children experience abuse.
"We have representatives from Denton Police Department and the (Caroline County) Sheriff's Office here," he said. "A lot of times, those cases start with their work. But as those children progress, they go to social service and then our advocates, which serve each one of those children."
Caroline County Circuit Court Judge Heather Price said in an interview that CASA reports offer an important perspective to judges.
"They give me a different angle than what the attorneys representing the parents would say or the attorneys representing the department," she said. "Here you have the voice of the child that's speaking through an advocate."
Before attendees of the ceremony fanned out to plant pinwheels, citations and awards were handed out. Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) presented CASA of Caroline with a citation in recognition of the Pinwheels for Prevention campaign.
Del. Jeff Ghrist (R-36, Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, and Caroline), who was also in attendance at the event, talked about the importance of the services CASA of Caroline offers children.
"In order to be able to connect them with that one person that they can trust, it takes a community to do that," he said. "It takes CASA to do that."
At the event, CASA of Caroline awarded the Caroline Career and Technology Center for the having highest participation across Caroline County Public Schools in coloring pinwheels to inspire hope from children experiencing abuse. Horn said 40% of CCTC students colored pinwheels. She said they will receive a Kona Ice party as their prize.
Career center Principal Courtney Handte said it means a lot to her and the center's staff that their students showed support for National Child Abuse Prevention Month, which is April.
"It's important for all students to know what is out there and available to them, and that they are not alone," Handte said. "Caroline County is a small community, but we are mighty. And we will surround them with the support and love that they need during challenging times."

title: Experts discuss Mid-Shore impacts of human trafficking
author: TOM MCCALL
content:
Experts discuss Mid-Shore impacts of human trafficking

 April 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 751
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Around 180 people attended the For All Seasons presentation on human trafficking on Tuesday night at the Avalon Theatre, where a panel of experts painted a picture of a changing landscape for trafficking crimes.With the increasing use of social media, traffickers find and groom their victims at home, a more methodical trust-gaining method than before the advent of the internet, they said.
According to Thomas Stack, anti-human trafficking and sexual assault response manager for Mayor's Neighborhood Office of Safety and Engagement for the City of Baltimore, because young people's lives are so transparent online, traffickers can target individuals who are alone, mad at their parents and not doing well in school. Low self esteem is the target, he said.
"It is all about getting the word out there. Human trafficking has been around a long time, but the awareness has probably only been around for the last 20 years," Stack said. "Maryland has a toxic mixture of both poverty and wealth. The poverty is a major risk factor for exploitation and the wealth is the buyers of sex, the people who are willing to purchase people for their pleasure."
Maryland is also geographically vulnerable to trafficking, the experts said.
"We are two hours from Philly, three hours from New York, we have a lot of sporting events, we have two major cities, and we have airports and casinos, everything a trafficker wants," Stack said. "Like we have the Preakness coming up. There will be a lot of males who have traveled here. The traffickers know that and will bring their victims of sex trafficking to service those males."
The speakers made it clear that human trafficking happens in the Mid-Shore community.
"There was a 15-year-old trafficked in Denton, so it is here," Stack said.
By becoming more aware of the problem, they said, community members can identify victims and reach out.
Heather Amador, deputy director of victim services policy and programs for the Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy, was one of the speakers. She said members of the community can look for signs of trafficking, like bruises, new tattoos and new suggestive clothing.
Red flags can also appear online, Stack said, like if a teenager has multiple Facebook profiles with some that have nothing to do with their family or friends.
"Human trafficking is here. People don't want to believe that their neighbors are capable of such things," Amador said. "A lot of human trafficking victims don't even identify as a victim. They see themselves as voluntarily engaging in it. They don't see the coercion that goes along with it. They are deceived to go down this path or forced into addiction. They think they are helping someone else out."
Amador had one victim in her office who simply said she needed to make money. She was a runaway and had nowhere to go, Amador said, and she needed housing.
Amador came across a case where a child had to perform a sex act to get lunch money in her lunch account and emphasized that that is trafficking too.
For All Seasons offers a host of services around human trafficking, from trainings, to getting the word out, to psychological services, to addiction services.
Beth Anne Dorman, CEO and president of For All Seasons, says it takes a village to combat trafficking.
"Our anti-human trafficking efforts focused on a team-based approach," she said. "We collaborate with law enforcement, first responders, Department of Social Services, child advocacy centers, school administrators, teachers and the hospital, officials from the towns and counties we serve."
Then she introduced a video of Maryland Comptroller Brooke Lierman, who created and helped pass legislation to make the Maryland Regional Navigator program when she was a legislator. This program supports survivors of trafficking. For All Seasons is a participant.
"Maryland recorded 118 cases of human trafficking involving 173 victims. This figure includes sex and labor exploitation. Child sex trafficking is also a concern. Since 2012 over 500 children have been identified by Child Protective Services as reportedly being trafficked in Maryland. This remains vastly under reported," Lierman said in the video.
She said she was committed to ensuring access to services for every survivor of sex trafficking in Maryland. She highlighted For All Seasons as "essential to the safety and wellness of our communities."
The night ended with a call to action for the audience.
"It is a hidden crime so we all have to be alert," said Susan Ahlstrom, regional navigator at For All Seasons. "We all have to be vigilant."
For more information on human trafficking and available resources, visit missingkids.org, polaris.com and netsmartz.com

title: Crime in Cambridge 'trending down,' police department says
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Crime in Cambridge 'trending down,' police department says

 April 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Crime 
 
 521
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The number of reported crimes, ShotSpotter alerts and shots fired calls is down in the first quarter of this year compared to last year in Cambridge, according to a quarterly report from the Cambridge Police Department.Cambridge Police Chief Justin Todd said he thinks this shows that crime in Cambridge is "trending down."
"A lot of credit goes to our officers that are out doing what we're asking of them to do as an administration," he said about these decreases. "And that's patrol with a purpose, be in our high-crime areas."
Todd also attributes the lowering of these stats to the department's work in getting guns off the street. He said that last year the department averaged getting one illegal firearm off the street per week in Cambridge alone.
"We know there's more out there, and we know there's still crime," Todd said. "But we're making progress."
According to the CPD report, in the first quarter of 2024, CPD submitted 200 crime incidents committed within its jurisdiction to the National Incident-Based Reporting System, a national reporting system for crimes used by police departments. That is compared to 247 incidents submitted in the first quarter of 2023.
This year, the majority of those incidents have been assaults.
The CPD report also states there was a 33.3% decrease in ShotSpotter alerts for the first quarter of 2024 compared to the first quarter of 2023. ShotSpotter is a gunshot detection system that has sensors that can detect and locate illegal gunfire incidents and alert law enforcement.
The CPD report states there was a 40.9% decrease in shots fire calls compared to the first quarter of 2023.
The first quarter of this year, there were 46 Shot Spotter alerts and 13 shots fired calls in Cambridge, according to the report. There was one shooting in that time.
Todd confirmed that shooting was on March 1 in the 800 block of Phillips Street. According to previous Dorchester Star reporting, police found several spent shell casings from multiple calibers of handguns on the scene. Isaiah David Foster, 23, of Cambridge was arrested on firearm possession charges, as well as resisting arrest and obstructing and hindering, following the incident.
According to the CPD report, calls for service increased 9.1% in the first quarter of 2024 compared to the first quarter of 2023. Todd said this is a good thing because it shows that officers are out in the community doing their jobs.
Compared to 171 adult arrests, there were eight juvenile arrests and 34 juvenile referrals in the first quarter of 2024.
Although Todd said he didn't have those numbers for this time last year, when it comes to juvenile crime, he thinks Cambridge is "stagnant."
"I think there's a lot of work to do with juvenile reform," he said. "We have to put more emphasis on figuring out why these kids are out committing these crimes and getting in touch with families by working through social services and Juvenile Services."
Todd said that the department will have a better understanding of the state of crime in Cambridge come summer.
"When the kids get out of school, that'll be a big factor of just how good we're doing crime-wise," he said.

title: After deadly work zone crashes, a push for change
author: SAPNA BANSIL Capital News Service
content:
After deadly work zone crashes, a push for change

 April 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: SAPNA BANSIL Capital News Service | Section: News 
 
 631
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — After a pair of deadly work zone incidents cast attention on the dangers of road work, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore enacted a set of protections for workers and their families that his administration describes as "a moral imperative."Hours after the state's legislature adjourned, a bill increasing fines for work zone speed violations and another covering educational costs for families of fallen workers were among the first measures from the 2024 session that Moore signed into law.
At a bill signing ceremony, Lt. Gov. Aruna Miller, a former transportation engineer, invoked two fatal crashes that inspired the new legislation. In March 2023, six highway workers died when a car careened into a work zone on Interstate 695. Nearly a year later, six construction workers repairing potholes atop the Francis Scott Key Bridge were killed when a container ship struck the bridge, causing it to collapse.
"The men and women in the construction industry place themselves in harm's way every day on the frontline of service," Miller said. "We saw it happen on March 22, 2023. And we saw it happen again on March 26, 2024. It's a moral imperative that we protect workers who provide critical service, public service for all of us."
Among the measures to receive Moore's signature was the Maryland Road Worker Protection Act, which Miller championed throughout the legislative session and touted Tuesday, during an event overlooking the site of the I-695 crash to mark National Work Zone Awareness Week.
Effective June 1, the new law permits the installation of multiple speed cameras within a single work zone and raises the fine for speed camera violations to $80. The current penalty in Maryland is $40, among the lowest such fines in the country.
Beginning January 2025, fines shift to a tiered system ranging from $60 to $500 depending on the driver's speed. Fines will double if workers are present at the time of the violation.
The new law is part of a larger effort to change driver behavior in work zones by strengthening enforcement methods and increasing education. Distracted driving, aggressive driving and speeding are the leading causes of work zone crashes, according to the State Highway Administration.
"Most crashes are not accidents," State Highway Administrator William Pines told Capital News Service. "In reality, they're very preventable. The majority of crashes that occur happen because of behaviors with drivers. So if we want to stop the root cause of most crashes, we've got to deal with driver behavior."
But the law offers no safety solutions for incidents like the collapse of the Key Bridge, which was unrelated to driver behavior. Maryland Transportation Secretary Paul Wiedefeld told Capital News Service on Tuesday that officials may consider structural solutions to bolster bridge safety but are awaiting the results of an investigation by the National Transportation Safety Board before making any specific policy proposals.
Instead, lawmakers responded to the bridge collapse by recognizing the toll that work zone crashes leave on workers' families.
In the final hours of the legislative session, the General Assembly passed the Protecting Opportunities and Regional Trade (PORT) Act, primarily aimed at providing emergency aid to workers and businesses affected by the closure of the Port of Baltimore.
Moore's administration offered a successful amendment to the bill creating the Fallen Transportation Workers Scholarship Program, providing tuition assistance for five years of full-time study or eight-years of part-time study to children and spouses of workers who have died on the job since 2022.
"What happened on the bridge is horrifically traumatic, and I think one of the things that we wanted to do is protect others who are in a similarly dangerous situation," said Maryland Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City), who co-sponsored the PORT Act.
"Certainly, we wish there were no one participating in that fund, but sadly, we know how dangerous this work is," he continued.

title: Tilghman man sentenced for child porn distribution, animal cruelty
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Tilghman man sentenced for child porn distribution, animal cruelty

 April 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Crime 
 
 346
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A Tilghman man was sentenced to 33 years with 10 years suspended for three counts of distribution of child pornography and one count of aggravated animal cruelty on Tuesday.Parker Greer Michael Matta, 21, was arrested by the Talbot County Sheriff's Office in March 2023 after detectives found evidence of child pornography on his electronic devices while executing a search warrant, police said.
The Sheriff's Office's Criminal Investigations Division received a tip from the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children involving Matta in March, according to previous Star Democrat reporting.
With assistance from the Howard County Police Department, the Sheriff's Office learned that Matta sent an image containing child pornography to another person via a social media platform in December 2022.
After reviewing the file, an investigator with the Talbot County Sheriff's office was able to identify an image depicting sexual abuse against a young female child between the ages of toddler and 5 years-old.
On March 31, 2023, the Talbot County Sheriff's Office executed a search warrant on Matta's residence, and found several electronic devices where images and videos of child pornography were located by investigators.
Additionally, investigators located several images depicting child sexual abuse that Matta shared to a group chatroom named "~Pxdo Paradise~" on an internet-based messaging and sharing application.
Also discovered in the investigation was a video wherein Matta sexually abused a labrador retriever at the Tilghman residence, leading to the defendant's conviction for aggravated animal cruelty.
Matta pled guilty to the distribution of child pornography charge on Nov. 29, according to court documents. In February, Matta's sentencing was postponed so that he could receive a psycho-sexual evaluation before being sentenced.
At the sentencing, Deputy State's Attorney Chelsea Endzel recommended the maximum sentence of 33 years with 10 years suspended, or 23 years to serve in prison.
"We are very happy with the outcome of this difficult case as it honors the trauma and harm suffered by the child victims in cases involving possession and distribution of Child Sexual Abuse Material and the threat that individuals who have a sexual interest in children pose to society," Endzel said.

title: Police: Two teen girls carjacked, assaulted 74-year-old woman
author: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com
content:
Police: Two teen girls carjacked, assaulted 74-year-old woman

 April 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com | Section: Crime 
 
 434
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Two females suspects, ages 16 and 18, are in custody after they allegedly assaulted and carjacked a 74-year-old woman in Perryville on Wednesday, April 24 — while she was doing them a favor, according to police.Investigators arrested the suspects after locating them and the stolen vehicle in York, Pennsylvania, on Thursday morning — about 12 hours after the carjacking, which occurred at approximately 7 p.m. Wednesday on Honaker Street near Keesey Lane, reported Chief Robert Nitz of the Perryville Police Department.
The suspects are awaiting extradition back to Cecil County, where both have been charged as adults with numerous criminal offenses, according to Nitz. (Juveniles who are at least 16 and are accused of committing certain serious crimes, including carjacking, automatically are charged as adults.)
Because officials cannot serve the two suspects with the charging documents until after extradition, Nitz declined to release their names on Thursday.
Police reported that the suspects approached the elderly woman in the Royal Farms parking lot in the 5400 block of West Pulaski Highway (Route 40) and asked her for a short ride in her Nissan Altima.
The victim obliged and started driving toward downtown Perryville, as the suspects had requested, police said. Then one of the suspects asked her to turn onto Honaker Street, and she did, police added.
"When they got to the end of Honaker Street, the suspect in the front seat asked her to stop and then both suspects demanded that she exit the vehicle. When she did, the two suspects assaulted the woman. They threw her to the ground and drove away in her car," Nitz outlined, before noting that PPD officers rushed to the scene at 7:06 p.m. after the incident was reported.
Paramedics reportedly gave the victim medical attention.
In addition to searching for the stolen vehicle and the suspects in Perryville and the surrounding area, officers broadcasted a be-on-the-lookout (BOLO) over the police radio, Nitz reported. In addition, investigators entered information about the stolen vehicle and the carjacking incident into two national crime databases, which proved to be beneficial in the investigation, according to Nitz.
Police located the stolen Nissan in York, Pa. while handling an incident that involved 10 suspects, including the two females who allegedly committed the carjacking in Perryville, Nitz reported.
Authorities in York contacted PPD early Thursday morning after matching the Nissan they had recovered to the stolen one that PPD investigators had entered in the national databases, according to Nitz.
Police in York charged the two suspects with possession of stolen property in that jurisdiction, Nitz said. PPD investigators filed numerous criminal charges, including carjacking, against the two suspects in Cecil County, he added.

title: After two deadly work zone crashes, Maryland officials press for change

After two deadly work zone crashes, Maryland officials press for change

Wes Moore enacted a set of protections for workers and their families that his administration describes as "a moral imperative."Hours after the state's legislature adjourned, a bill increasing fines for work zone speed violations and another covering educational costs for families of fallen workers were among the first measures from the 2024 session that Moore signed into law.

In March 2023, six highway workers died when a car careened into a work zone on Interstate 695. Nearly a year later, six construction workers repairing potholes atop the Francis Scott Key Bridge were killed when a container ship struck the bridge, causing it to collapse.
"The men and women in the construction industry place themselves in harm's way every day on the frontline of service," Miller said. "We saw it happen on March 22, 2023. And we saw it happen again on March 26, 2024. It's a moral imperative that we protect workers who provide critical service, public service for all of us."
